questions.stem:
In the context of DBMS, consider the two sets $\mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{S}$ given below.

T: I: Logical schema; II: Physical schema; III: External schema.
S: L: Views; M: File organization and indexes; N: Relations.

Which one of the following is the correct match from $\mathbf{T}$ to $\mathbf{S}$?

steps.title: The three levels of a database description
steps.body: A database is described at three levels. The external schema is what one group of users sees: a view, which is a stored query that shows only some columns and rows. The logical schema describes the whole database to the DBMS and to designers: the relations, their attributes, keys and constraints. The physical schema says how those relations sit on disk: file organization (heap, sorted, hashed) and indexes. The rule: the higher the level, the closer to the user and the further from the disk.

steps.title: Match each level
steps.body: External schema (III) is views, so III-L. Logical schema (I) is the set of relations, so I-N. Physical schema (II) is file organization and indexes, so II-M.

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: I-N, II-M, III-L is option (C). In option (A) the logical level is called views and the external one relations; in (B) the physical level is called views; in (D) the physical level is called views and the external level indexes. Each wrongly puts a disk or user-level word at the other end.

traps.text: Calling the logical schema "views" and the external schema "relations". Views are the user-facing level, relations are the designer-level description of the whole database.
Matching the physical schema to views and the logical schema to file organization. Indexes and file organization are storage details, so they are physical, not logical.
Putting indexes with the external schema. Users never see indexes; they only feel their effect on speed, which is a physical-level concern.

shortcut.body: Start from the one pair you cannot forget: indexes belong to the physical level, so II-M. Only option (C) has II-M together with a sensible rest (III-L, views are what users see). About 30 seconds.

recognize.clues: The words logical schema, physical schema and external schema, matched with views, file organization and indexes, and relations, are the three levels of database description.
recognize.contrast: Do not mix this with the ER model or with normalization: those decide what the relations should be, while this question only asks which level of description a given object belongs to.

check.body: Test each pairing by deletion. Dropping an index changes no query result, only speed, so it is physical. Dropping a view changes what one user group can see, so it is external. Dropping a relation changes what the database contains at all, so it is the logical level.

solutionDiagram.alt: Three stacked boxes: external schema (views) on top, logical schema (relations) in the middle, physical schema (file organization and indexes) at the bottom.

sources.label: GATE 2026 CS-2 answer key, IIT Guwahati

hints.text: Each item in the first set is a way of describing the same database. Ask who looks at each description: an end user, a designer, or the storage engine.
A database is described at three layers: the part a user group sees, the part that describes the whole database, and the part that describes bytes on disk.
The closer a description is to the disk, the more it talks about files and access paths. The closer to the user, the more it talks about what a particular group is allowed to see.
Sort the three items in the second set by the same test: which one a user could never notice except through speed, which one is a stored query, and which one is the table structure itself.

questions.stem:
Consider a relational database schema with two relations $R(P, Q)$ and $S(X, Y)$.

Let $E = \{\langle u\rangle \mid \exists v\, \exists w\, \langle u, v\rangle \in R \wedge \langle v, w\rangle \in S\}$ be a tuple relational calculus expression.

Which one of the following relational algebraic expressions is equivalent to $E$?

steps.title: Read the calculus as a recipe
steps.body: A pair $\langle a, b\rangle \in R$ means a row of $R$ whose first column ($P$) is $a$ and second column ($Q$) is $b$. The same variable written twice forces equal values. The expression asks for every $u$ for which some $v$ and some $w$ exist with $\langle u,v\rangle$ in $R$ and $\langle v,w\rangle$ in $S$. The rule: a variable that occurs in two places is a join condition; a variable that is quantified away and not output is projected out.

steps.title: Map variables to columns
steps.body: In $\langle u,v\rangle \in R$: $u$ is $P$ and $v$ is $Q$. In $\langle v,w\rangle \in S$: $v$ is $X$ and $w$ is $Y$. So the shared variable $v$ ties $R.Q$ to $S.X$, and only $u$, that is $P$, is output.
steps.tex: u = R.P,\quad v = R.Q = S.X,\quad w = S.Y

steps.title: Write the algebra and match
steps.body: The join condition is $R.Q = S.X$, which is the same as $S.X = R.Q$, and the output is $\Pi_P$. A join is symmetric, so the order of $R$ and $S$ does not matter. That is option (B). Options (A) and (C) join on $R.P$, which is $u$, and (D) joins on $S.Y$, which is $w$.

traps.text: Joining $R.P$ to $S.X$. That uses the first column of $R$ for the shared variable, but the shared variable $v$ is the second column of $R$.
Joining $R.P$ to $S.Y$: both sides are wrong, since $R.P$ is $u$ and $S.Y$ is $w$, which share no variable.
Joining $S.Y$ to $R.Q$. The left side is right ($R.Q$ is $v$) but $S.Y$ is $w$, the free variable; $v$ is $S.X$.

shortcut.body: Find the variable that appears twice: $v$. It sits in the second slot of $R$ ($Q$) and the first slot of $S$ ($X$). Look for the option that equates $Q$ with $X$ and projects $P$: only (B). Order of the two relations in a join is irrelevant.

recognize.clues: The expression is written as a set of tuples with existential quantifiers and angle-bracket membership in R and S, and the options are projection and join expressions, so the task is translating calculus to algebra.
recognize.contrast: Do not read it as a selection query: no constant is compared, only a shared variable, so the algebra needs a join rather than a selection.

check.body: Run a one-row instance. Let R = {(1,2)} and S = {(2,9)}. The calculus gives u=1 with v=2 and w=9, so E = {1}. Try the join equalities on this instance: only the one that equates R.Q with S.X finds a matching pair, and projecting P then gives 1. An equality on R.P or on S.Y finds no pair and returns the empty set.

sources.label: GATE 2026 CS-1 answer key, IIT Guwahati

solutionDiagram.alt: R(P,Q) and S(X,Y) joined by a line labelled Q = X; the output is the P column of R.

hints.text: Look for a letter that appears in both angle brackets of the calculus expression. What must be true of the two rows that carry it?
In tuple relational calculus written with angle brackets, each position in a bracket stands for a column of that relation, in the order the schema lists them.
A variable used in two relations becomes an equality between those two columns, which is a join condition. A variable that is quantified and never output is dropped by projection.

Label the positions: in the pair from R, the first slot is P and the second is Q; in the pair from S, the first slot is X and the second is Y. Then say which slots carry the repeated variable and which slot carries the output variable.

questions.stem:
Consider two relations describing $teams$ and $players$ in a sports league:

- $teams(tid, tname)$: $tid$, $tname$ are team-id and team-name, respectively
- $players(pid, pname, tid)$: $pid$, $pname$, and $tid$ denote player-id, player-name and the team-id of the player, respectively

Which ONE of the following tuple relational calculus queries returns the name of the players who play for the team having $tname$ as 'MI'?
options: $\{p.pname \mid p \in players \wedge \exists t\,(t \in teams \wedge p.tid = t.tid \wedge t.tname = \text{'MI'})\}$
$\{p.pname \mid p \in teams \wedge \exists t\,(t \in players \wedge p.tid = t.tid \wedge t.tname = \text{'MI'})\}$

steps.title: How a tuple calculus query is built
steps.body: A query $\{ x.\text{attr} \mid \text{condition}\}$ says: collect $x.\text{attr}$ for every tuple variable $x$ that satisfies the condition. Writing $x \in \text{rel}$ makes $x$ range over the rows of that relation, so $x$ can only use the attributes of that relation. $\exists t$ introduces a second variable. The rule that decides this question: the output variable must range over the relation that holds the output attribute, and two relations are connected only by an explicit equality on their common attribute.

steps.title: Build the query for this question
steps.body: The output is a player name, so $p$ ranges over $players$ (only $players$ has $pname$). We need a team $t$ in $teams$ whose name is MI and whose id equals the player's team id.
steps.tex: \{p.pname \mid p \in players \wedge \exists t\,(t \in teams \wedge p.tid = t.tid \wedge t.tname = \text{'MI'})\}

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (B) and (D) let $p$ range over $teams$ and then ask for $p.pname$, but $teams$ has no $pname$ attribute, so they are not queries on this schema. (C) has the right ranges but no link between $p.tid$ and $t.tid$: if any team is MI, every player is returned, even one of another team. Only (A) is correct.

traps.text: Having the join equality but swapping the relations: $p$ ranges over $teams$, which has no $pname$, and $t$ ranges over $players$, which has no $tname$.
Forgetting the join. Without $p.tid = t.tid$ the condition "some MI team exists" does not depend on $p$, so all players come back whenever MI exists.
Both slips together: wrong relation for the output variable and no join equality.

shortcut.body: Spot the join equality $p.tid = t.tid$. Only (A) and (B) have it, and (B) asks for $pname$ from $teams$, which has no such column. So (A), in about 40 seconds.

recognize.clues: The query is asked in tuple relational calculus form with an output list, a range for each tuple variable and an existential variable, over two relations joined by a shared team id.
recognize.contrast: Do not treat it as plain selection: the name condition lives in a different relation from the output, so a join equality on the team id is needed, which a single-relation selection never has.

check.body: Test on teams = {(1, MI), (2, CSK)} and players = {(10, Ann, 1), (11, Bob, 2)}. A correct query returns only Ann, because her team id matches the MI team. A query that drops the equality on team id returns both Ann and Bob, since some MI team exists. A query that asks for a player name from teams fails to be defined at all.

sources.label: GATE 2025 CS-1 final answer key, IIT Roorkee

hints.text: Which relation holds the column you must output, and which relation holds the condition on the team name? Can one tuple variable serve both?
In tuple relational calculus a variable written with membership in a relation can use only the attributes of that relation. The output list is also written in terms of such variables.
Two relations are linked only by an explicit equality between a column of one and a column of the other. Without that equality the existential part does not depend on the output variable at all.

Pick the range of the output variable from the relation that has the output column. Pick the range of the second variable from the relation that has the team name. Then write the equality that ties them together, and read each option for those three things.

variation.stem: Consider two relations: $teams(tid, tname)$ and $players(pid, pname, tid)$, where $tid$ is the team id of a player. Which ONE of the following tuple relational calculus queries returns the names of the teams that have a player named 'Raj'?
options: $\{t.tname \mid t \in teams \wedge \exists p\,(p \in players \wedge p.tid = t.tid \wedge p.pname = \text{'Raj'})\}$
$\{t.tname \mid t \in players \wedge \exists p\,(p \in teams \wedge p.tid = t.tid \wedge p.pname = \text{'Raj'})\}$
variation.explanation: The output is a team name, so $t$ ranges over $teams$, and the name condition is on a player, so $p$ ranges over $players$. The equality $p.tid = t.tid$ ties the player to the team. Option B swaps the ranges, so it asks for a column the relation lacks. Option C has no join and returns every team whenever any Raj exists. Option D has both faults.

questions.stem: In the context of owner and weak entity sets in the ER (Entity-Relationship) data model, which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The weak entity set MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship
The owner entity set MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship
Both weak and owner entity sets MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship
Neither weak entity set nor owner entity set MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body: A weak entity set has no key of its own. Each weak entity is identified by combining its owner's key with a partial key (discriminator). The identifying relationship is the relationship that links a weak entity to its owner. Total participation of a set in a relationship means every entity of that set takes part in it at least once; partial means some may not.

steps.title: The deciding rule
steps.body: A weak entity's key contains the owner's key, so a weak entity with no owner would have no identity and could not be stored. Hence every weak entity must be related to an owner: the weak set participates totally. An owner, in contrast, can exist with no dependents (an employee with no children), so the owner side may be partial.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only the weak side is forced to be total. That is option (A).

traps.text: Reversing the roles: it is the weak set that is forced, not the owner. An owner with no dependents is perfectly legal.
Assuming both sides are tied together because the relationship has a double diamond. The double diamond marks identification, and the only forced total side is the weak one.
Thinking participation is always a free choice. For the weak set it is not, since its key is built from the owner's key.

shortcut.body: Ask who cannot live without whom. A dependent cannot exist without its owner, so the weak side is total; the owner can exist alone. Pick (A).

recognize.clues: The stem names owner and weak entity sets and the identifying relationship, and asks which side must participate totally, which is the defining property of a weak entity.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse it with generalization or with cardinality constraints: a one-to-many ratio says how many, while total participation says whether every entity must take part at all.

check.body: Check through the relational translation. The table for the weak set has the owner key as part of its primary key, and primary key columns cannot be null. So every weak row names an owner, which is total participation. The owner table has no column that points to its dependents, so an owner with none is legal.

solutionDiagram.alt: Owner connected by a single line to a double-diamond identifying relationship, which connects by a double line to a double-bordered weak entity set.

hints.text: Think of one weak entity in the real world, such as a dependent of an employee. Can it be described without mentioning the other entity?
A weak entity set has no key of its own. What it needs for identification comes from the entity set it depends on, joined with a partial key.
Identification is what a key provides. For each side in turn, ask what happens to its key if the other side is missing from the picture.
For each side in turn, ask: can an entity of this set exist while taking part in no identifying relationship at all? Then compare the answers for the owner and the weak set with the four statements.

variation.stem: A Loan entity set is identified by loan_no. A Payment entity set has only a partial key, installment_no, and each payment is identified by its loan together with its installment number, through an identifying relationship Pays. In the ER model, which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: Every Payment entity must take part in Pays, but a Loan may have no payments
Every Loan must have at least one payment, but a Payment may exist without a loan
Both Loan and Payment must take part in Pays
Neither Loan nor Payment is forced to take part in Pays
variation.explanation: Payment is the weak set: its key contains loan_no, so a payment with no loan has no identity. That forces total participation of Payment. A newly granted loan can have no payments yet, so Loan may participate partially. Option A states exactly this; the others reverse the roles or force or free both sides.

questions.stem:
The relation schema, Person(pid, city), describes the city of residence for every person uniquely identified by pid. The following relational algebra operators are available: selection, projection, cross product, and rename.

To find the list of cities where at least 3 persons reside, using the above operators, the minimum number of cross product operations that must be used is

steps.title: What a cross product can see
steps.body: Selection, projection and rename work on one row at a time (or on a pair, after a cross product). With no cross product, a condition looks at one person. With $k$ copies joined by $k-1$ cross products, a condition can compare $k$ persons at once. Counting is not an operator, so "at least 3 persons" has to be expressed by naming three different persons of the same city.

steps.title: Three persons need three copies
steps.body: Rename Person three times as $R$, $S$, $P$ and form $R \times S \times P$. Select the rows where the three cities are equal and the three pids are pairwise different, then project city. A city survives exactly when three distinct persons live in it.

steps.title: Why one product is not enough
steps.body: With one product the query sees two persons. A city holding exactly two persons and a city holding three persons look identical to every condition on a pair: both contain a pair with equal city and different pids. So no expression with one cross product can separate "at least 3" from "at least 2". Three copies need $3-1 = 2$ products. Answer (B).

traps.text: One product feels enough because "same city" is a pair test. But a pair cannot tell two residents from three.
Writing 3 because the threshold is 3. Three copies of the relation need only two cross products between them.
Counting products as if every comparison between copies needed its own product. The selection applies all comparisons at once.

shortcut.body: Persons compared at once $= $ products $+ 1$. Need 3 persons, so 2 products. Do not map "3" to the number of products. For "at least $n$" the answer is $n-1$.

recognize.clues: Only selection, projection, cross product and rename are allowed, and the query needs a count threshold (at least 3), so the count has to be built by comparing several renamed copies of the same relation.
recognize.contrast: Do not reach for aggregation or division: those are not in the allowed list, and without them the only way to express a count is to name distinct rows with extra copies.

check.body: Test the three-copy query on a city with exactly two persons. There is no triple of pairwise different pids, so the city is not output. A city with three persons has such a triple and is output. A two-copy query returns the two-person city too, so it cannot separate the cases. That is why the count of copies, not the count of conditions, is the minimum.

solutionDiagram.alt: Three renamed copies of Person joined by two cross product signs, followed by a selection of equal cities and different pids, then projection on city.

hints.text: The operators listed have no counting. So how can a query still tell three persons from two? Think about what a condition can look at in one go.
A cross product of copies of a relation lets one condition compare rows from the different copies together. Renaming is what lets you tell the copies apart.
A condition can only relate as many rows as there are copies in the product. With fewer copies than the threshold, a city with fewer residents looks the same as a city with enough.
Decide how many different persons the condition must name for the city to qualify, then count the products needed to bring that many copies of the relation together.

variation.stem: The relation schema Person(pid, city) gives the city of residence of every person, identified by pid. Only selection, projection, cross product and rename are available. To find the cities where at least 4 persons reside, the minimum number of cross product operations that must be used is
variation.explanation: Four distinct persons of one city have to be named in the same condition, so four renamed copies of Person are needed. Joining four copies takes $4-1=3$ cross products. Two products join three copies, enough for triples only, and one product gives pairs only. Option D counts copies instead of products.

questions.stem: Let S be the specification: "Instructors teach courses. Students register for courses. Courses are allocated classrooms. Instructors guide students." Which one of the following ER diagrams CORRECTLY represents S?
questions.figure: Four ER diagrams (i) to (iv). All have rectangles Instructor, Course, Classroom and diamonds Teaches (Instructor-Course), Allocation and Guides. (i): Registration is a rectangle attached to Course, Student is a diamond joining Course and Guides, and Classroom is joined to Allocation. (ii): there is no Student; a rectangle Projects sits between Guides and Registration, and Registration (diamond) joins Course and Projects. (iii): Course-Registration-Student, Instructor-Guides-Student, but Classroom is joined directly to Course by a line and Allocation hangs from Course unconnected to Classroom. (iv): Instructor-Teaches-Course, Course-Registration-Student, Instructor-Guides-Student, Course-Allocation-Classroom.

diagram.alt: Four ER diagrams (i) to (iv) over Instructor, Course, Classroom, Student or Projects with relationship diamonds Teaches, Allocation, Registration and Guides.

steps.title: Nouns and verbs
steps.body: In an ER diagram a thing that has attributes of its own is an entity set (a rectangle) and an association between things is a relationship (a diamond). In the sentence, the nouns are Instructor, Course, Student and Classroom; the verbs teach, register, allocate and guide give four relationships. The rule: each sentence must appear as a diamond joining exactly the two entity sets it names.

steps.title: List what the diagram must contain
steps.body: Teaches joins Instructor and Course. Registration joins Student and Course. Allocation joins Course and Classroom. Guides joins Instructor and Student. Four rectangles, four diamonds, eight lines, and nothing else.

steps.title: Check each candidate
steps.body: (i) makes Student a diamond and Registration a rectangle, so it swaps entity and relationship. (ii) has no Student entity at all and introduces Projects, which the specification never mentions. (iii) joins Classroom straight to Course and leaves Allocation unattached, so the allocation sentence is not represented as a relationship between the two. (iv) has all four relationships with the right ends. Answer (D).

traps.text: Reading the shapes by position instead of type. In (i) Student is a diamond and Registration is a rectangle, which turns an entity into a relationship.
Not noticing the extra entity Projects. Registration is joined to Projects, so students and their registration are not represented.
Seeing Classroom connected to Course and stopping. The connection must pass through the Allocation diamond; here it bypasses it.

shortcut.body: Eliminate by the entity list: Student missing in (ii), Student drawn as a diamond in (i), Allocation not between Course and Classroom in (iii). About a minute with the picture.

recognize.clues: The question gives a short specification in words and asks which diagram represents it, so each noun becomes an entity set and each verb phrase becomes a relationship between two of them.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse a relationship with an attribute or an entity: Registration and Allocation look like things, but in this specification they only record that a student takes a course or a classroom is given to a course.

check.body: Count the lines. Four relationships with two ends each give exactly eight entity-to-diamond lines, and every line must join a diamond to a rectangle. A diamond with a dangling end, a diamond joined to another diamond, a rectangle where a diamond belongs or an entity that the text never names each break this count or this rule.

solutionDiagram.alt: The correct ER diagram: Instructor, Course, Student and Classroom with relationship diamonds Teaches, Registration, Allocation and Guides.

hints.text: Read the specification sentence by sentence. For each sentence, which two things does it connect, and is that connection a thing or an association?
An ER diagram uses rectangles for entity sets and diamonds for relationships. Each relationship diamond is joined by lines to the entity sets that take part in it.
A correct diagram has one diamond per association, and each diamond is joined to exactly the two entity sets named in its sentence. Shapes must not be swapped, and no entity may be added or dropped.

Make a checklist from the text: four entity sets and four relationships, with the two ends of each. Then test every diagram against the checklist for missing or extra shapes, wrong shape types and diamonds with a missing end.

variation.stem: Let S be the specification: "Authors write books. Readers borrow books. Books are shelved in sections. Librarians assist readers." Which one of the following descriptions of an ER diagram CORRECTLY represents S?
options: Rectangles Author, Book, Reader, Section, Librarian; diamonds Writes (Author-Book), Borrows (Reader-Book), Shelved (Book-Section), Assists (Librarian-Reader)
The same, except that Reader is drawn as a diamond and Borrows as a rectangle
The same, except that there is no Librarian entity and Assists is a diamond joining Reader and Book
The same, except that Section is joined to Book by a plain line and the Shelved diamond has only its Book end
variation.explanation: Five nouns give five rectangles and four verbs give four diamonds, each joined to the two entity sets named in its sentence. Option B swaps an entity and a relationship. Option C removes the Librarian entity the text names and rewires Assists. Option D leaves Shelved with one end, so the shelving is not a relationship between book and section.

questions.stem:
Consider the following two relations, $R(A,B)$ and $S(A,C)$:

$R = \{(10,20), (20,30), (30,40), (30,50), (50,95)\}$
$S = \{(10,90), (30,45), (40,80)\}$

The total number of tuples obtained by evaluating the following expression $\sigma_{B<C}(R \bowtie_{R.A=S.A} S)$ is ______.

steps.title: What the operators do
steps.body: A theta join $R \bowtie_{\theta} S$ pairs every row of $R$ with every row of $S$ and keeps the pairs that satisfy $\theta$. The selection $\sigma_{B<C}$ then keeps only the pairs where $B$ is smaller than $C$.

steps.title: Join on A
steps.body: $R$ has $A$ values 10, 20, 30, 30, 50 and $S$ has 10, 30, 40. Matching: $A=10$ gives (10,20) with (10,90); $A=30$ gives (30,40) and (30,50), each with (30,45). The values 20, 50 (in $R$) and 40 (in $S$) find no partner. Three joined rows.

steps.title: Apply B < C
steps.body: $20<90$ keeps the first row. $40<45$ keeps the second. $50<45$ fails. Two rows remain, so the answer is 2.

traps.text: Answering 3, the size of the join, and forgetting that the selection removes the row with $B=50$, $C=45$.
Answering 5 or 15 by counting a full cross product of 5 and 3 rows instead of joining on $A$.
Answering 1 by testing only one of the two $A=30$ rows of $R$; both of them join with the single $S$ row.

shortcut.body: Only $A = 10$ and $A = 30$ occur in both relations, so at most three rows exist: list them and test $B<C$. Total time under a minute.

recognize.clues: The expression is a selection applied over a theta join on equal A, with both relations listed in full, so the task is to join by hand and then filter the joined rows.
recognize.contrast: Do not read it as a cross product followed by a selection on A alone; it is the same result, but starting from the cross product hides that only matching A values can contribute.

check.body: Count from the side of $S$ instead. The row (10,90) meets $R$ row (10,20), and $20<90$ holds: 1. The row (30,45) meets (30,40) and (30,50); only $40<45$ holds: 1. The row (40,80) meets no $R$ row with $A=40$: 0. The total is 1+1+0=2.

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of the three joined rows with a column showing B < C: true, true, false, giving two kept rows.

hints.text: Which rows of R can find a partner in S at all? Check the values of the joining column first, before looking at B and C.
A theta join on equal values of A pairs each row of R with every row of S that carries the same A value; a row with no matching A contributes nothing.
The selection is applied to the joined rows, so first list all joined rows, and only then keep the ones for which the comparison between the two later columns holds.
List the values of A that appear in both relations. For each, write the pairs of R rows and S rows, giving the joined rows with their B and C values.
Only two values of A occur in both relations, and one of them appears twice in R, so the join has a small, countable list of rows. Write them out and test B against C in each.

variation.stem:
Consider the relations $R(A,B)$ and $S(A,C)$:

$R = \{(1,5), (2,6), (2,9), (3,4), (7,8)\}$
$S = \{(2,7), (3,10), (2,8), (9,1)\}$

The total number of tuples obtained by evaluating $\sigma_{B<C}(R \bowtie_{R.A=S.A} S)$ is ______.
variation.explanation: Only $A=2$ and $A=3$ occur in both. For $A=2$ the pairs are $B\in\{6,9\}$ with $C\in\{7,8\}$, which gives 4 joined rows, of which $6<7$ and $6<8$ pass. For $A=3$, $4<10$ passes. The total is 3.

questions.stem: Which one of the options given below refers to the degree (or arity) of a relation in relational database systems?
options: Number of attributes of its relation schema.
Number of tuples stored in the relation.
Number of entries in the relation.
Number of distinct domains of its relation schema.

steps.title: Two sizes of a relation
steps.body: A relation is a table. Its columns are attributes and its rows are tuples. Two sizes are used: the degree (also called arity) is the number of columns, and the cardinality is the number of rows. The degree is fixed by the schema; the cardinality changes as tuples are inserted and deleted.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: The degree is the number of attributes of the schema: option (A). (B) is the cardinality. (C), the number of entries, would be degree times cardinality. (D) counts domains, but two attributes may share a domain (two integer columns share one), so it is not the degree.

traps.text: The number of tuples is the cardinality. Students mix the two because "degree" sounds like a count of records.
Entries (cells) number degree times cardinality; this is neither of the two named sizes.
Distinct domains can be fewer than attributes, since many attributes can draw from the same domain.

shortcut.body: Degree = columns, cardinality = rows. Choose the option that says attributes.

recognize.clues: The words degree and arity ask for a size of the relation as a schema-level quantity, in a list of options that count different things in a table.
recognize.contrast: Cardinality is the look-alike size: it counts rows and changes with the data, while the degree counts columns and is fixed by the schema.

check.body: Test on a concrete table with 3 columns and 5 rows. Its degree is 3, its cardinality is 5 and it holds 3*5=15 cells. Two columns drawn from the same domain still count twice toward the degree, so the number of distinct domains can be smaller than the degree and cannot be the degree. Adding a row moves 5 and 15 but leaves 3.

sources.label: GATE 2023 CS answer key, IIT Kanpur

hints.text: Picture a relation as a table. Two different counts can be taken from it. Which one stays the same while rows are added and deleted?
A relation has columns, called attributes, and rows, called tuples. The schema fixes the columns, and the contents of the table change over time as rows come and go.

Try two operations on the table: inserting a row, and adding a column with ALTER TABLE. For each kind of count, note whether either operation changes it, and recall which part of a relation the schema controls.
For each of the four options, decide whether it counts columns, rows, cells or something else, then compare with the property that is fixed by the schema alone.

variation.stem: A relation Book(isbn, title, author, price) currently stores 250 tuples. The attributes isbn, title and author draw on the string domain and price on the decimal domain. Which one of the following is the degree of the relation Book?
variation.explanation: The degree is the number of attributes of the schema: isbn, title, author and price make 4. The value 250 is the cardinality, 1000 is the number of cells (degree times cardinality) and 2 is the number of distinct domains, which undercounts because attributes sharing a domain still count separately. Inserting more tuples would change 250 but never 4.

questions.stem:
Consider the following three relations in a relational database.

$Employee(\underline{eId}, Name)$, $Brand(\underline{bId}, bName)$, $Own(\underline{eId}, \underline{bId})$

Which of the following relational algebra expressions return the set of $eId$s who own all the brands?

steps.title: What "owns all brands" means
steps.body: Division $A / B$ returns the values of the attributes of $A$ not in $B$ that appear in $A$ together with every tuple of $B$. Here $\Pi_{eId,bId}(Own) / \Pi_{bId}(Brand)$ returns every $eId$ paired in Own with all bIds of Brand. The same idea in basic operators: take every employee-brand pair that should exist, remove those that do exist, and the employees left over are the ones missing some brand.

steps.title: Option A and B
steps.body: (A) is division by the full list of brands, which is the definition. (B) builds the set of all pairs (employee who owns something) $\times$ (all brands), subtracts Own to get missing pairs, projects the employees who are missing something, and subtracts them from the employees. Employees who own all brands remain. Both are correct. A script ran both on 3000 random instances and each matched a direct check.

steps.title: Option C and D fail
steps.body: (C) divides by the brands that appear in Own. If a brand is owned by nobody, it is missing from the divisor, and an employee who owns every owned brand is returned although a brand remains. (D) divides a product of employee and owned-brand pairs, which contains every pair, by Brand. The quotient includes every employee in Own whenever all brands are owned by somebody, whether or not that employee owns them. Both are wrong. Answer: A and B.

traps.text: Choosing (C) because the division shape is right. The divisor $\Pi_{bId}(Own)$ drops brands nobody owns, so it tests "owns all owned brands".
Choosing (D) because it also has a product and a division. The product already pairs every employee with every owned brand, so the division by Brand then holds for all of them.
Ruling out (B) because it has no division sign. It is the same query written with difference only, and it is correct.

shortcut.body: Divisor must be Brand, never Own: (C) and (D) are out. Keep the two options that use Brand correctly: (A) is the textbook division and (B) is the "none missing" form.

recognize.clues: The words "own all the brands" are a for-all over Brand, and Own is the table of employee and brand pairs, which is the shape of a dividend in a division.
recognize.contrast: A plain join or selection returns employees who own some brand. Only division, or the difference form that removes employees with a missing pair, tests every brand.

check.body: Take Brand = {b1, b2} and Own = {(e1,b1), (e1,b2), (e2,b1)}, so only e1 owns all brands. Run each option and compare with {e1}. Then add a brand b3 that nobody owns and run again: options that read the brand list from Own now behave differently from those that read it from Brand.

solutionDiagram.alt: Grid of employees e1 to e4 against brands b1 to b3 with marks for ownership; only e1 and e3 have all three marks.

sources.label: GATE 2022 CS answer key, IIT Kharagpur

hints.text: Say "owns all the brands" as a statement about missing brands: what must be true of the brands an employee does not own?
Division $A / B$ keeps the left-side values that appear in $A$ paired with every row of $B$. It is the relational form of a for-all query.
A for-all test is only as strong as the list it ranges over. A list drawn from a relation that can leave members out checks a weaker claim than the full list.
Try each option on two small cases. In the first, there are two brands and nobody owns the second. In the second, every brand is owned by someone, and one employee owns only some of them.

In the first case an employee holding only the first brand is missing a brand, so a correct expression must not return that employee. In the second case the employee who owns only some brands must also be left out. One case alone does not remove every wrong option.

variation.stem:
Consider the relations $Student(\underline{sId}, sName)$, $Course(\underline{cId}, cName)$ and $Takes(\underline{sId}, \underline{cId})$.

Which of the following relational algebra expressions return the set of $sId$s of students who take all the courses?
variation.explanation: Dividing by the full course list is the definition, and the last option subtracts the students who miss some pair, so both are correct. Dividing by $\Pi_{cId}(Takes)$ ignores courses nobody takes. The third option subtracts pairs in the wrong direction, so it removes nothing useful and returns every student who takes any course. A random-instance check agreed: only options 2 and 4 always matched the direct test.

questions.stem:
A relation $r(A, B)$ in a relational database has $1200$ tuples. The attribute $A$ has integer values ranging from $6$ to $20$, and the attribute $B$ has integer values ranging from $1$ to $20$. Assume that the attributes $A$ and $B$ are independently distributed.

The estimated number of tuples in the output of $\sigma_{(A>10)\vee(B=18)}(r)$ is ______.

steps.title: Selectivity
steps.body: The selectivity of a condition is the fraction of tuples that satisfy it. With values spread evenly, a condition that accepts $k$ of the $n$ possible values has selectivity $k/n$. Independence means the selectivity of "this and that" is the product of the two. For "this or that", use inclusion-exclusion: $P(X \vee Y) = P(X) + P(Y) - P(X \wedge Y)$.

steps.title: Fractions
steps.body: $A$ takes 15 values (6 to 20). $A>10$ means 11 to 20: 10 values, so $P = 10/15 = 2/3$. $B$ takes 20 values, so $P(B=18) = 1/20$.

steps.title: The other accepted value
steps.body: If $r$ is viewed as a set with one row per distinct pair ($15 \times 20 = 300$ pairs), the same fraction gives $300 \times 41/60 = 205$. The official key accepts 819 to 820 and 205.

traps.text: Adding $2/3 + 1/20$ without subtracting the overlap, which gives $1200 \times 43/60 = 860$.
Taking 20 values for $A$ because $B$ has 20. $A$ runs 6 to 20, which is 15 values, so $A>10$ is $2/3$ and not $1/2$.
Multiplying the two fractions instead of using inclusion-exclusion for $\vee$: $1200 \times (2/3)(1/20) = 40$ is the estimate for $\wedge$, not $\vee$.

shortcut.body: Count the complement instead: a tuple fails only if $A \le 10$ (prob $1/3$) and $B \ne 18$ (prob $19/20$), which is $19/60$. So the answer is $1200 \times (1 - 19/60) = 820$.

recognize.clues: The phrases "estimated number of tuples" and "independently distributed" with value ranges ask for a selectivity estimate, not a row count, and the OR in the condition calls for inclusion-exclusion.
recognize.contrast: A join size estimate divides by the number of distinct join values. Here one relation is filtered, so only the selectivity of the condition matters.

check.body: Count over the grid of distinct value pairs: $15 \times 20 = 300$ pairs. Pairs with $A>10$ number $10 \times 20 = 200$. Pairs with $A \le 10$ and $B=18$ number $5 \times 1 = 5$. The union has $205$ pairs, a share of $205/300 = 41/60$, which must equal the share found by the fraction method.

solutionDiagram.alt: Grid of A from 6 to 20 against B from 1 to 20 with the cells A greater than 10 and the row B equals 18 shaded: 205 of 300 cells.

sources.label: GATE 2021 CS-1 answer key, IIT Bombay

hints.text: The condition joins two tests with OR. What share of the tuples passes each test alone, and how do the two groups overlap?
Selectivity is the share of tuples that pass a condition. With evenly spread values, a test accepting $k$ of $n$ values has selectivity $k/n$.
For independent attributes an AND multiplies the shares. An OR needs inclusion-exclusion, or one minus the share that fails both tests.
Count how many values each attribute can take, remembering that both ends of an integer range are included. Then count how many of those pass its own test.
For $A$, the values run from 6 to 20 and the test $A>10$ keeps 11 to 20. Write that as a fraction of the values $A$ can take.

variation.stem:
A relation $r(A, B)$ has $2400$ tuples. The attribute $A$ has integer values from $3$ to $12$ and the attribute $B$ has integer values from $1$ to $15$. Assume $A$ and $B$ are independently distributed.

The estimated number of tuples in the output of $\sigma_{(A>8)\vee(B=4)}(r)$ is ______.
variation.explanation: $A$ has 10 values and $A>8$ keeps 9 to 12, so $P(A>8)=4/10$. $B$ has 15 values, so $P(B=4)=1/15$. By inclusion-exclusion $P = 4/10 + 1/15 - (4/10)(1/15) = 0.44$, and $2400 \times 0.44 = 1056$. Adding the two shares without removing the overlap gives 1120, which is the usual slip.

questions.stem:
The following relation records the age of $500$ employees of a company, where $empNo$ (indicating the employee number) is the key:

$empAge(\underline{empNo}, age)$

Consider the following relational algebra expression:

$\Pi_{empNo}\big(empAge \bowtie_{(age>age1)} \rho_{empNo1,age1}(empAge)\big)$

What does the above expression generate?
options: Employee numbers of only those employees whose age is the maximum.
Employee numbers of only those employees whose age is more than the age of exactly one other employee.
Employee numbers of all employees whose age is not the minimum.
Employee numbers of all employees whose age is the minimum.

steps.title: Rename and theta join
steps.body: $\rho_{empNo1,age1}(empAge)$ makes a second copy of the table with columns renamed, so the table can be compared with itself. The theta join with condition $age > age1$ pairs each row $x$ of the first copy with every row $y$ of the second copy for which $x.age > y.age$. The projection keeps $empNo$ of the first copy, and as a set each employee number appears once, however many partners it has.

steps.title: Who survives
steps.body: An employee $x$ appears in the output exactly when some $y$ is strictly younger. That fails only for employees whose age equals the minimum age: nobody is younger. So the output is all employees except those of minimum age.

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: "All employees whose age is not the minimum" is option (C). (A) and (D) name the extremes. (B) says "exactly one other", but the join keeps anyone with one or more younger partners. A test on five employees with ages 30, 25, 25, 40, 18 returned everyone but the 18-year-old.

traps.text: Reading the greater-than as selecting the oldest. The condition only needs some younger partner, which most employees have.
Treating each pair as a count. Projection of a set removes the duplicates, so an employee with many younger partners still appears once and is not limited to one.
Reversing the comparison: the minimum-age employees are exactly the ones that are left out.

shortcut.body: Read $age>age1$ as "there is someone younger". Everyone who is not the youngest passes, so the youngest (minimum) drops out: (C).

recognize.clues: The same relation appears twice, the second time under a rename $\rho$, and the join condition compares an attribute with its renamed copy using an inequality.
recognize.contrast: An equijoin on the key would pair every row only with itself. The inequality makes it a self-join that separates the rows at one extreme age from all the others.

check.body: Use the smallest instance that has a tie: ages 20, 20 and 30. The pairs that satisfy $age>age1$ are the 30 with each of the two 20s. Only the 30 reaches the output, so the tied rows at the bottom both drop out together. A single employee gives an empty join.

solutionDiagram.alt: Employees ordered by age in a chain; all except the youngest appear in the output of the self join.

sources.label: GATE 2021 CS-1 answer key, IIT Bombay

hints.text: Take one row of the first copy. What must be true of some row in the second copy for that pair to survive the join?
Renaming makes a second copy so a table can be compared with itself. A theta join keeps only the pairs that satisfy the comparison, and projecting onto a key removes duplicates.
A row appears in the output when at least one partner passes the comparison. So ask which rows have no partner at all, not which have many.
Try five employees aged 22, 35, 35, 50 and 41. For each one, list the rows of the second copy it can pair with under the condition.
Run the oldest of your five first and note whether it forms any pair. Then run the youngest and do the same.

variation.stem:
The relation $empAge(\underline{empNo}, age)$ records the age of $300$ employees, where $empNo$ is the key. Consider the expression

$\Pi_{empNo}\big(empAge \bowtie_{(age<age1)} \rho_{empNo1,age1}(empAge)\big)$

What does it generate?
options: Employee numbers of only those employees whose age is the minimum.
Employee numbers of all employees whose age is not the maximum.
Employee numbers of only those employees whose age is the maximum.
Employee numbers of only those employees whose age is less than the age of exactly one other employee.
variation.explanation: A row survives when some other row is strictly older. Only the employees of maximum age have no older partner, so they drop out and everyone else stays. Projection removes duplicates, so having many older partners does not matter. A simulation on 2000 random age lists matched this rule every time.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is used to represent the supporting many-one relationships of a weak entity set in an entity-relationship diagram?

steps.title: The four drawing symbols
steps.body: In an ER diagram a rectangle is an entity set, a diamond is a relationship, and an oval is an attribute. A double border means the thing is special: a double rectangle is a weak entity set (it has no key of its own), a double oval is a multivalued attribute, and a double diamond is an identifying relationship. A single underline inside an oval marks a key attribute, and a dashed underline marks the partial key of a weak set.

steps.title: Which symbol supports a weak set
steps.body: A weak entity set depends on its owner through a many-one relationship (many weak entities to one owner). That supporting relationship is the identifying relationship, drawn as a diamond with a double or bold border. So the answer is (A).

steps.title: Eliminate the rest
steps.body: (B) is the weak entity set itself, not its relationship. (C) is a multivalued attribute. (D) is a key attribute. None of these is a relationship.

traps.text: Double rectangles draw the weak entity set. The question asks for its supporting relationship, which is a diamond.
A double oval is a multivalued attribute, which has nothing to do with identification.
An underlined identifier marks a key attribute of a strong set; a weak set has only a partial key.

shortcut.body: The question says "relationships", and relationships are diamonds. Only (A) is a diamond.

recognize.clues: The words "weak entity set" and "supporting many-one relationship" ask for the notation that ties a weak set to its owner.
recognize.contrast: Do not mix up the weak entity set itself with the relationship that identifies it. The question asks about the link, not the set.

check.body: Test each option by what the shape connects. A relationship joins two entity sets, so it must be a diamond; only option (A) has a diamond. Then confirm the border: an identifying relationship is the one that carries the weak set to its owner, and it is drawn with a double border. A plain diamond would be an ordinary relationship, so the double border in (A) fits the supporting link.

solutionDiagram.alt: A weak entity set drawn as a double rectangle joined by a double line to a double diamond, which links to the owner entity set.

sources.label: GATE 2020 CS answer key, IIT Delhi

hints.text: A weak entity set and its supporting link are two different things in the diagram. Which of the two is the question asking you to draw?
An ER diagram uses one shape for entity sets, one for relationships and one for attributes. A double or bold border marks the weak or special version of that shape.
A weak set has no key of its own, so it is identified through an owner. The link that carries this identification is a many-to-one relationship from the weak set to its owner.
Write each option as shape, border and content, and say what kind of thing that shape stands for. Cross out the options that stand for something other than a link between two sets.
Ovals always draw attributes, whatever their border or underline, so none of the oval options can be the link.

variation.stem: In an entity-relationship diagram, which symbol is used to draw the partial key (discriminator) of a weak entity set?
variation.explanation: The partial key is an attribute, so it is an oval. A weak set has only a partial key, which tells weak entities of one owner apart, so it is underlined with a dashed line. A solid underline marks the key of a strong set, a double oval marks a multivalued attribute, and the double rectangle is the weak set itself.

questions.stem:
Consider the following relations $P(X,Y,Z)$, $Q(X,Y,T)$ and $R(Y,V)$.

How many tuples will be returned by the following relational algebra query?

$\Pi_X\big(\sigma_{(P.Y=R.Y \wedge R.V=V2)}(P \times R)\big) - \Pi_X\big(\sigma_{(Q.Y=R.Y \wedge Q.T>2)}(Q \times R)\big)$

steps.title: Operators
steps.body: A cross product pairs every row of one relation with every row of another. A selection keeps the pairs that meet a condition. A projection keeps some columns and removes duplicates, since a relation is a set. A set difference $A - B$ keeps the elements of $A$ not in $B$. The query is a difference of two projected sets of X values, so each side is a set of X values.

steps.title: Left side
steps.body: Keep $P \times R$ rows with $P.Y = R.Y$ and $R.V = V2$. $R$ rows with $V2$ are (Y3,V2) and (Y2,V2). $P$ has $Y2$ in (X2,Y2,Z2), matching (Y2,V2); no $P$ row has $Y3$. So the left side is $\{X2\}$.

steps.title: Right side
steps.body: Keep $Q \times R$ rows with $Q.Y = R.Y$ and $Q.T > 2$. $Q$ rows with $T>2$ are (X1,Y2,5) and (X1,Y1,6). They match (Y2,V3), (Y2,V2) and (Y1,V1). The projected X values are $\{X1\}$.

steps.title: Difference
steps.body: $\{X2\} - \{X1\} = \{X2\}$, which has one tuple. The answer is 1.

traps.text: Answering 2 by adding the two sides instead of subtracting them: $\{X2\} \cup \{X1\}$ has 2 tuples. The operator between the projections is a difference.
Answering 0 by dropping the condition $Q.T>2$. Then $Q \times R$ keeps every $Q$ row whose $Y$ is in $R$, the right side becomes $\{X1, X2, X3\}$, and it removes $X2$ from the left.
Reading $Q.T>2$ as $T \ge 2$ adds (X2,Y1,2) to the right side, so it becomes {X1, X2} and the answer drops to 0. Read the comparison exactly.

shortcut.body: Skip the cross products. Left: which $P$ rows have a $Y$ that is paired with $V2$ in $R$ ($Y2$ or $Y3$)? Only $X2$. Right: which $Q$ rows with $T>2$ have a $Y$ in $R$? Both have X1. Subtract.

recognize.clues: A projection stands on each side of a minus, each side selects from a cross product by equating the shared attribute $Y$, and the output is counted as a set.
recognize.contrast: An intersection or join would keep $X$ values found on both sides. The minus keeps only those found on the left side alone.

check.body: Recompute the right side straight from the rows of $Q$ with $T>2$, which are (X1,Y2,5) and (X1,Y1,6). Each has a $Y$ that occurs in $R$, so the right side is $\{X1\}$ and $X2$ never appears in it. Now test the one left-side value: $X2$ is absent from the right side, so it survives the difference and the count is 1.

solutionDiagram.alt: Left set {X2} from P joined with R, right set {X1} from Q joined with R, and their set difference {X2} with one tuple.

hints.text: The query subtracts one set of $X$ values from another. Work out each side as a plain list of $X$ values before you subtract.
A selection keeps rows that meet a condition, a projection keeps chosen columns and drops duplicates, and a product followed by an equality on $Y$ acts like a join on $Y$.
Set difference removes from the left set every value that also appears on the right. An $X$ survives only if the right side never produces it.
Skip building the full products. For each side, find the rows of $R$ that satisfy its condition, then find the rows of the other relation that share their $Y$ value.
On the left side, write down the $Y$ values of the rows of $R$ that carry $V2$.

variation.stem:
Consider the relations $P(X,Y,Z)$, $Q(X,Y,T)$ and $R(Y,V)$ with the tuples below.

$P$: (X1,Y2,Z1), (X2,Y2,Z2), (X3,Y1,Z3), (X3,Y3,Z4)
$Q$: (X1,Y1,2), (X2,Y3,1), (X3,Y2,6), (X4,Y3,7)
$R$: (Y1,V1), (Y2,V2), (Y3,V2), (Y3,V3)

How many tuples will the following query return?

$\Pi_X\big(\sigma_{(P.Y=R.Y \wedge R.V=V2)}(P \times R)\big) - \Pi_X\big(\sigma_{(Q.Y=R.Y \wedge Q.T>2)}(Q \times R)\big)$
variation.explanation: The rows of $R$ with $V2$ have $Y2$ and $Y3$, and $P$ rows with those $Y$ values give the left set $\{X1, X2, X3\}$. In $Q$ only (X3,Y2,6) and (X4,Y3,7) have $T>2$ and a matching $Y$ in $R$, so the right set is $\{X3, X4\}$. The difference is $\{X1, X2\}$, which has 2 tuples.

questions.stem:
In an Entity-Relationship (ER) model, suppose $R$ is a many-to-one relationship from entity set $E1$ to entity set $E2$. Assume that $E1$ and $E2$ participate totally in $R$ and that the cardinality of $E1$ is greater than the cardinality of $E2$.

Which one of the following is true about $R$?
options: Every entity in $E1$ is associated with exactly one entity in $E2$.
Some entity in $E1$ is associated with more than one entity in $E2$.
Every entity in $E2$ is associated with exactly one entity in $E1$.
Every entity in $E2$ is associated with at most one entity in $E1$.

steps.title: Two ideas
steps.body: Many-to-one from $E1$ to $E2$ means each $E1$ entity is related to at most one $E2$ entity, while an $E2$ entity may have many $E1$ partners. Total participation of a set means every entity of that set is related to at least one entity. Cardinality here is the number of entities in the set.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: $E1$ is on the "many" side with a limit of one partner, and total participation forces at least one. So every $E1$ entity has exactly one $E2$ partner: $R$ is a function from $E1$ onto the entities that have partners, and since $E2$ is total, every $E2$ entity has a partner too.

steps.title: Use the size condition
steps.body: $|E1| > |E2|$ and every $E1$ entity maps to exactly one $E2$ entity, so by the pigeonhole principle some $E2$ entity has at least two $E1$ partners. That kills (C) and (D). (B) is impossible since an $E1$ entity has at most one partner. Only (A) is true.

traps.text: Reading many-to-one the wrong way round. An $E1$ entity can have only one partner in $E2$.
Taking "total" to mean one-to-one. Since $|E1|>|E2|$, some $E2$ entity must have two $E1$ partners.
At most one partner for $E2$ describes one-to-many from $E2$ to $E1$, the opposite direction; with more $E1$ than $E2$ entities it is false.

shortcut.body: Many-to-one plus total on the many side gives "exactly one" for every $E1$ entity: option (A). The rest contradict many-to-one or the size condition.

recognize.clues: The terms "many-to-one", "participate totally" and a comparison of the sizes of the two sets fix how many partners each entity has, and the sizes then force a pigeonhole conclusion.
recognize.contrast: Total participation is not one-to-one: it only gives at least one partner. A many-to-one from $E1$ to $E2$ is also not one-to-many, which swaps the roles of the two sets.

check.body: Build the smallest model: $E1$ with three entities, $E2$ with two, each $E1$ entity linked to one $E2$ entity and every $E2$ entity used at least once. List all such assignments. Each leaves some $E2$ entity with two partners, and none gives an $E1$ entity two partners. Any option contradicted by this model is out.

solutionDiagram.alt: Four E1 entities each with one arrow to one of two E2 entities, so each E2 entity receives two arrows.

hints.text: Turn the two phrases about participation and direction into a statement about how many partners each entity of $E1$ and of $E2$ must have.
In a many-to-one relationship from $E1$ to $E2$, each $E1$ entity has at most one partner. Total participation means every entity of that set has at least one partner.
Count partners from the side of the larger set. If every entity there has exactly one partner and the other set has fewer entities, what must happen to some entity of the smaller set?
Write three facts: partners per $E1$ entity, partners per $E2$ entity, and the size comparison. Then test each option against all three.
Count the links of $R$ by summing over the entities of $E1$, then compare that total with the number of entities of $E2$, each of which needs at least one link.

variation.stem:
In an ER model, $R$ is a many-to-one relationship from entity set $E1$ to entity set $E2$. Both sets participate totally in $R$, and $E1$ and $E2$ have the same finite number of entities.

Which one of the following is true about $R$?
options: Some entity in $E2$ is associated with more than one entity in $E1$.
Every entity in $E2$ is associated with exactly one entity in $E1$.
Some entity in $E1$ is associated with no entity in $E2$.
Every entity in $E1$ is associated with more than one entity in $E2$.
variation.explanation: Every $E1$ entity has exactly one partner, and every $E2$ entity has at least one because of total participation. With equal sizes, the pairing is one-to-one. Enumerating all such relations on 3 and on 4 entities per set gave only perfect matchings, so no $E2$ entity has two partners and none has none.

questions.stem:
Consider the relations $r(A, B)$ and $s(B, C)$, where $s.B$ is a primary key and $r.B$ is a foreign key referencing $s.B$. Consider the query

$Q: r \bowtie (\sigma_{B<5}(s))$

Let $LOJ$ denote the natural left outer-join operation. Assume that $r$ and $s$ contain no null values.

Which one of the following queries is NOT equivalent to $Q$?

steps.title: Join versus left outer join
steps.body: The natural join keeps only pairs that match on $B$. The left outer join keeps every row of the left relation, and a row with no match is padded with NULL on the right side. Because $r.B$ is a foreign key to the primary key $s.B$ and has no nulls, every $r$ row has exactly one $s$ partner, so $r \bowtie s$ and $r\ LOJ\ s$ are the same relation. Equivalent queries return the same rows for every legal instance.

steps.title: A, B and D
steps.body: $Q$ keeps rows of $r$ whose $B$ is below 5 together with their $s$ row. (A) joins first and filters on $B<5$: same rows. (B) works the same, since the LOJ equals the join. (D) filters $r$ first and then LOJs with all of $s$; each remaining row finds its partner, so no padding occurs and the rows are the same.

steps.title: C differs
steps.body: (C) keeps every row of $r$. For a row with $B \ge 5$ the partner was removed by $\sigma_{B<5}(s)$, so the row stays, padded with NULL in $C$. $Q$ drops such rows, so (C) returns extra tuples. Example: $r=\{(1,7)\}$, $s=\{(7,9)\}$: $Q$ is empty, (C) gives $(1,7,\text{NULL})$. Answer (C).

traps.text: (A) is equivalent: join then filter gives the same rows as filter then join, because the filter is on the shared attribute $B$.
(B) looks risky because of the LOJ, but the foreign key guarantees a partner for every $r$ row, so it behaves like a join.
(D) filters $r$ on $B$ and LOJs with all of $s$; the foreign key guarantees partners, so nothing is padded.

shortcut.body: The only query that applies the filter to $s$ and then pads with LOJ is (C); padding brings back the rows the filter was meant to remove. The others filter after or at the left side.

recognize.clues: A join with a filtered copy of one relation is compared against rewrites that use a left outer join, under a primary-key and foreign-key guarantee and with no nulls.
recognize.contrast: Filtering after a left outer join drops the padded rows, while filtering one input before it keeps them. A selection moves freely through an inner join and into the preserved side of a left outer join, but pushing it into the null-supplying side ($s$ here) keeps the unmatched $r$ rows padded with NULL.

check.body: Use $r=\{(1,7),(2,3)\}$ and $s=\{(7,9),(3,4)\}$. The query $Q$ returns only $(2,3,4)$. Evaluate every option on this instance: the three equivalent ones return only $(2,3,4)$, and the one that is not equivalent also returns $(1,7,\text{NULL})$.

hints.text: Equivalent means the same rows on every legal instance. Look for the option where the filter and the outer join can disagree about which rows stay.
A natural join keeps matching pairs only. A left outer join keeps every left row and pads the missing right values with NULL.
The foreign key gives each $r$ row exactly one partner in the full $s$. That fact tells you when an outer join behaves like a plain join and when it does not.
For each option, ask whether the filter on $B$ reaches $s$ before the join or the result after it, and whether an outer join can then pad a row.
Take one row of $r$ whose $B$ value is not below 5. Run every option on it and write which options still return a row.

Consider the relations $r(A, B)$ and $s(B, C)$, where $s.B$ is a primary key and $r.B$ is a foreign key referencing $s.B$. Consider the query

Let $LOJ$ denote the natural left outer join. Assume $r$ and $s$ contain no null values.

variation.explanation: The foreign key gives each $r$ row one partner in $s$, so joining first and then filtering on $C$ keeps the same rows, and so does the left outer join followed by the filter. The last option filters $s$ first and then pads, so an $r$ row whose partner has $C \le 5$ stays with NULL in $C$, while $Q$ drops it. questions.stem: An ER model of a database consists of entity types $A$ and $B$. These are connected by a relationship $R$ which does not have its own attribute. Under which one of the following conditions, can the relational table for $R$ be merged with that of $A$?
options: Relationship $R$ is one-to-many and the participation of $A$ in $R$ is total
Relationship $R$ is one-to-many and the participation of $A$ in $R$ is partial
Relationship $R$ is many-to-one and the participation of $A$ in $R$ is total
Relationship $R$ is many-to-one and the participation of $A$ in $R$ is partial

steps.title: Merging a relationship table
steps.body: A relationship between $A$ and $B$ is stored as a table of pairs of keys. It can be merged into the table of one entity by adding a foreign key column there. A column holds one value, so this works only for the side that has at most one partner. If that column can be NULL for some rows the merge is not clean; total participation guarantees a value in every row.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.body: The side with a single partner is the "many" side of a many-to-one relationship. Here that means $R$ many-to-one from $A$ to $B$: each $A$ has at most one $B$, so $A$ gets a column holding the key of $B$. $R$ has no attributes of its own, so nothing else needs to move. With total participation of $A$ every $A$ row has a value, so no NULL arises.

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: The condition is many-to-one with $A$ total: option (C). One-to-many puts the single partner on the $B$ side, so the column belongs in $B$, not $A$ (options A and B). Many-to-one with $A$ partial (D) leaves NULLs, so (C) is the clean answer.

traps.text: One-to-many means each $A$ may have many $B$s, so $A$ cannot hold them in one column.
Same direction mistake, and the partial participation adds NULLs on top.
Correct direction but partial participation: the foreign key in $A$ would be NULL for $A$ entities with no $B$, which the textbook rule avoids.

shortcut.body: Merge goes to the "many" side and needs total participation to avoid NULLs: many-to-one with $A$ total. Answer (C).

recognize.clues: The question asks when the table for $R$ can be merged with that of $A$, and $R$ has no attributes of its own, so it is about where a foreign key can replace a separate relationship table.
recognize.contrast: A many-to-many relationship always keeps its own table. Only the side with at most one partner can absorb the relationship, so compare the roles of $A$ and $B$ first.

check.body: Take $A=\{a_1,a_2\}$ and $B=\{b_1\}$. Many-to-one with $A$ total gives pairs $(a_1,b_1)$ and $(a_2,b_1)$, so a column $bId$ in the table of $A$ holds one value in each row with no NULL. Under one-to-many, $a_1$ could pair with $b_1$ and $b_2$, which needs two values in one cell. With $A$ partial, an $a_2$ with no partner leaves NULL in that column.

solutionDiagram.alt: A many-to-one relationship R from A to B with total participation of A, and the merged table A with a foreign key column for B.

A column holds one value per row, so an entity row can carry a foreign key to its partner only if it has at most one partner.
Participation decides whether that column can be empty. Total participation fills it in every row, while partial participation may leave NULLs.
For each option, decide which of $A$ and $B$ has at most one partner under the stated cardinality, then check whether $A$ takes part totally or partially.
Read the cardinality from the side of $A$: how many $B$ entities can one $A$ entity have under one-to-many, and under many-to-one?

options: $S$ is many-to-one from $P$ to $Q$ and the participation of $Q$ in $S$ is partial
$S$ is one-to-many from $P$ to $Q$ and the participation of $Q$ in $S$ is total
$S$ is many-to-one from $P$ to $Q$ and the participation of $Q$ in $S$ is total
$S$ is one-to-many from $P$ to $Q$ and the participation of $Q$ in $S$ is partial
variation.explanation: One-to-many from $P$ to $Q$ means each $Q$ entity has at most one $P$ partner, so $Q$ can hold the key of $P$ in one column. Total participation of $Q$ means that column is never empty. With many-to-one from $P$ to $Q$ the single value would belong in $P$, and partial participation of $Q$ would leave NULLs.

questions.stem:
Consider a database that has the relation schemas $EMP(EmpId, EmpName, DeptId)$, and $DEPT(DeptName, DeptId)$. Note that the $DeptId$ can be permitted to be NULL in the relation $EMP$. Consider the following queries on the database expressed in tuple relational calculus.

(I) $\{t \mid \exists u \in EMP\,(t[EmpName] = u[EmpName] \wedge \forall v \in DEPT\,(t[DeptId] \ne v[DeptId]))\}$
(II) $\{t \mid \exists u \in EMP\,(t[EmpName] = u[EmpName] \wedge \exists v \in DEPT\,(t[DeptId] \ne v[DeptId]))\}$
(III) $\{t \mid \exists u \in EMP\,(t[EmpName] = u[EmpName] \wedge \exists v \in DEPT\,(t[DeptId] = v[DeptId]))\}$

Which of the above queries are safe?

steps.title: What safe means
steps.body: A tuple calculus expression is safe when it returns a finite result for every database, with every value in the result drawn from the database itself. An unsafe expression such as $\{t \mid \neg(t \in EMP)\}$ describes infinitely many tuples, because nothing ties $t$ to a stored tuple. The working rule used here: a query is safe when every quantifier ranges over a stored relation and $t$ is tied to a stored tuple by an equality. A strict textbook reading goes further and asks the same of every component of $t$.

steps.title: Read the three queries
steps.body: In all three, $t[EmpName]$ is tied to the name of an existing employee $u$, so the names in the result are stored values and the number of possible names is finite. The conditions on $t[DeptId]$ only restrict the department id.

steps.title: The department id
steps.body: (III) ties the id to a stored id by equality. (I) and (II) restrict $t[DeptId]$ only by inequality against $v \in DEPT$, so a strict textbook reading would not tie that component to a stored value, and the NULL note in the paper does not change that. The official key still counts all three queries as safe, so for the exam the rule stays: $t$ is anchored by $t[EmpName] = u[EmpName]$ to a stored employee, and $DeptId$ is only compared with the finite relation $DEPT$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: All three are safe: option (D).

traps.text: Dropping (III) because it looks different. It is the cleanest case: equality to a stored id.
Dropping (II) because "exists a department with a different id" feels unbounded. Its names are still tied to stored employees.
Dropping (I) because "for all departments, different" feels like negation. The note about NULL DeptId is given so that (I) is read as safe.

shortcut.body: Each query pins the name to an existing employee name. Take the key at face value: all three are safe, option (D). Under a stricter textbook reading, a bare "not equal" on a free attribute is a warning sign, so do not spend time on it; D is the official answer.

recognize.clues: The question asks which tuple calculus expressions are safe, and the three queries differ only in how $t[DeptId]$ is compared with $v[DeptId]$ for $v$ in $DEPT$: $\forall$ with $\ne$, $\exists$ with $\ne$, and $\exists$ with $=$.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse safety with equivalence of queries or with correctness of the result: a safe query can still return a surprising answer, and the question asks only whether the result is finite and drawn from stored values.

check.body: Take $EMP = \{(1, Ann, 10), (2, Bob, NULL)\}$ and $DEPT = \{(CS, 10)\}$. In every query $t[EmpName]$ must equal Ann or Bob, so at most 2 names can appear, and the only department id ever compared with $t[DeptId]$ is 10 from $DEPT$. Query (III) forces $t[DeptId] = 10$, so its result has at most the 2 tuples (Ann, 10) and (Bob, 10). Queries (I) and (II) use the same name candidates and the same single comparison value, which is the exam's anchoring rule at work; the bare inequality on $DeptId$ is the part a strict reading questions. The unsafe $\{t \mid \neg(t \in EMP)\}$ has no name candidates at all.

hints.text: What would go wrong if a query described infinitely many tuples? Ask which part of $t$ in each query is pinned to something stored.
A tuple calculus query is called safe when its result is always finite and built only from values that already sit in the database.

Quantifiers that range over a stored relation keep the search finite; ask through which equality the answer tuple $t$ is anchored to a stored tuple, and what each remaining condition on $t$ is compared against.
For each of the three queries, list how $t[EmpName]$ is fixed and how $t[DeptId]$ is constrained, and note which relation each quantified variable ranges over.

variation.stem:
Consider the relation schema $R(a, b)$. Consider the following queries in tuple relational calculus.

(I) $\{t \mid \neg(t \in R)\}$
(II) $\{t \mid \exists u \in R\,(t[a] = u[a] \wedge t[b] = u[b])\}$
(III) $\{t \mid t \in R \wedge \exists u \in R\,(u[a] = t[b])\}$

Which of the above queries are safe?
variation.explanation: Query (I) asks for every tuple not in $R$, which is infinite, so it is unsafe. Query (II) copies each tuple of $R$ and query (III) keeps only tuples that already belong to $R$, so both return a finite set of stored tuples.

questions.stem:
Consider a database that has the relation schema $CR(StudentName, CourseName)$. An instance of the schema $CR$ is as given below.

The following query is made on the database.

$T1 \leftarrow \pi_{CourseName}(\sigma_{StudentName=\text{SA}}(CR))$
$T2 \leftarrow CR \div T1$

The number of rows in $T2$ is ______.

steps.title: Division
steps.body: Division $A \div B$ returns the values of the attributes of $A$ that are not in $B$ and appear in $A$ together with every tuple of $B$. Here $CR \div T1$ gives every student who is paired in $CR$ with all the courses of $T1$. Extra courses do not disqualify a student; only a missing course does.

steps.title: Compute T1
steps.body: Student SA takes CA, CB and CC, so $T1 = \{CA, CB, CC\}$.

steps.title: Test each student
steps.body: SA has CA, CB, CC: yes. SB has CB, CC (no CA): no. SC has CA, CB, CC: yes. SD has CA, CB, CC, CD: yes, the extra CD is allowed. SE has CD, CA, CB (no CC): no. SF has CA, CB, CC: yes. So $T2 = \{SA, SC, SD, SF\}$, 4 rows.

traps.text: Answering 3 by leaving out SA. SA satisfies the condition against its own course set.
Answering 3 by excluding SD because it takes an extra course CD. Division requires a superset, not equality.
Answering 6, the number of students, or 5 by counting SE who has CD but is missing CC.

shortcut.body: Write the course set of each student and check that it contains {CA, CB, CC}: SA, SC, SD, SF. Count 4. Do not forget SA itself.

recognize.clues: The query $CR \div T1$ where $T1$ is a projected set of courses, and the question counts the students who are paired with all of those courses.
recognize.contrast: Division is not a natural join or an intersection: a join keeps students having any matching course, while division keeps only those having every course of the divisor.

check.body: Run the definition backwards by the formula $\pi_{S}(CR) - \pi_{S}((\pi_{S}(CR) \times T1) - CR)$ in words: a student is removed exactly when some course of $T1$ is missing from that student. Six students minus the two with a missing course (SB lacks CA, SE lacks CC) gives the same count.

solutionDiagram.alt: Matrix of the six students against courses CA to CD with marks; SA, SC, SD and SF have all of CA, CB and CC.

hints.text: Which students would the query keep? Think of what the second operand asks every kept student to have.
Division finds the values on one side that are paired, in the first relation, with every row of the divisor.
A student qualifies when the divisor set is contained in that student's own set of courses; having extra courses does not matter.
First work out the divisor relation from the selection on one named student, then write each student's course set and test containment.
The divisor is the set of courses taken by the named student, which has three courses. Students missing any one of them are out.
